question: Can the action of nonlinear neural-network activations be interpreted exactly as lifting inputs into an infinite monomial feature space, and can that view yield architecture conversion and equation-solving alternatives to gradient-based training?

key_findings.claim: The paper's valid core observation is only a bounded-domain approximation statement: a suitable continuous activation can be approximated by polynomials, so an activated affine form can be approximated by weighted input monomials.
key_findings.evidence: The proposed construction first truncates a Fourier series over a prescribed interval and then truncates the sine and cosine Taylor series. Substituting the resulting polynomial into an affine preactivation produces monomial interactions. This is an approximation whose degree and error depend on the chosen interval and truncations, not an exact global identity.

anchors.section: 2.1 Polynomial Approximation of Any Activation Function

key_findings.claim: The asserted exact infinite-power-series representation fails for ReLU and is not established for the paper's other named activations over the whole real line.
key_findings.evidence: The paper assumes that arbitrarily accurate polynomial approximation makes an activation equal to one infinite-degree polynomial. A convergent power series defines an analytic function on the interior of its convergence domain, whereas ReLU is nondifferentiable at zero; sigmoid and tanh Taylor series also have finite radii around a fixed center because of complex singularities. Periodic Fourier extension plus local Taylor truncation does not prove a single global power-series identity. The displayed Maclaurin formulas additionally print the sine series for both sine and cosine.

key_findings.claim: Even when a monomial expansion exists, one neuron is not an arbitrary hyperplane in that feature space because its coefficients are tightly coupled by the activation and a single affine weight vector.
key_findings.evidence: The paper expands one neuron as the sum over i of c_i times (a_0 plus a dot f)^i, then labels the result a Super Plane over all monomials. Multinomial expansion fixes every degree-i coefficient through the same c_i and products of the same affine weights; finite width gives a finite sum of such constrained ridge-function coefficient tensors. No spanning, rank, independence, or identifiability argument is supplied.

key_findings.claim: The claimed conversion of any trained CNN into any smaller chosen network is unsupported and generally false without capacity, domain, and approximation-error qualifications.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.4 proposes replacing activations by polynomials, matching coefficients in a one- or two-layer network, and thereby compressing a CNN into any desired architecture. It neither proves that the resulting nonlinear coefficient system has a solution nor accounts for the rank and depth needed to represent the target polynomial or piecewise-linear map. Max pooling is also called a polynomial even though a maximum of polynomials is generally only piecewise polynomial.

key_findings.claim: Recasting fitting as a multivariate nonlinear equation system is an algebraic reformulation, not a demonstrated reduction in computational complexity.
key_findings.evidence: The paper suggests coefficient matching followed by a generic fsolve call and concludes that neural-network training complexity is reduced to solving higher-degree nonlinear equations. It gives no complexity bound, existence or uniqueness condition, conditioning analysis, comparison with gradient descent, or scaling experiment; exact polynomial-system solving can itself be intractable and a chosen architecture may not interpolate the requested target.

key_findings.claim: The numerical section verifies hand-designed polynomial identities but does not test the paper's claims about modern activations, deep networks, compression, learning, or generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Experiments 1 and 2 select a one-hidden-layer four-node network with the square activation and solve coefficients for two quadratic targets; Experiment 2 prints correct outputs for only two inputs. Experiment 3 uses a fourth-power activation and reports scores on all four rows used to construct the target. Experiment 4 presents equations but no numerical result. No ReLU, sigmoid, CNN, real benchmark, held-out split, optimizer baseline, error curve, runtime, or approximation-degree study appears.

key_findings.claim: Several advertised applications are proposals rather than results.
key_findings.evidence: The one-dot categorical architecture is not defined mathematically or tested; the whole-integer parity example is only an intuition about periodic activations; the MNIST construction is asserted without an implementation; and the conclusion explicitly says more experiments are needed. The linked code repository returned HTTP 404 at review time, leaving only the short Octave snippets printed in the PDF available for inspection.

method.core_idea: View activation as a lift from affine input coordinates into coordinates indexed by all input monomials, making a neuron linear in a formally infinite feature vector and suggesting direct coefficient matching as an alternative to ordinary training.
method.mechanism: Approximate an activation on a selected range with a truncated Fourier expansion whose trigonometric terms are replaced by truncated Taylor polynomials; expand the activated affine form into monomials; call the ambient monomial basis Super Space and each neuron output a Super Plane; then choose target polynomials and solve the resulting nonlinear equations for network weights with a generic numerical root solver.
assumptions: Every activation of interest is adequately represented by the proposed Fourier-then-Taylor construction on the preactivation range encountered by the network.
An arbitrarily accurate sequence of approximations can be treated as exact equality to one infinite-degree polynomial.
Infinite sums, layer composition, and multinomial expansion can be interchanged without a convergence analysis.
A finite dataset and finite precision justify truncating the infinite monomial feature map without an explicit error bound.
The constrained coefficient tensors generated by the chosen width and depth can match the desired target polynomial.
The resulting nonlinear system has a numerically accessible solution and solving it is preferable to loss minimization.
Polynomial interpolation of training rows is an adequate objective for classification and regression generalization.

techniques.role: Approximates an activation over a prescribed interval with finitely many sine and cosine terms.
Replaces trigonometric terms by finite Taylor polynomials to obtain an ordinary polynomial activation surrogate.
Expands powers of affine preactivations into a formal feature vector indexed by input monomials.
Equates coefficients of a chosen target polynomial and a polynomial-activation network.
Uses a generic nonlinear equation solver to find one numerical network parameterization.
Constructs per-class negative polynomial distances whose largest output identifies a training class.

evaluations.setting: A synthetic two-class problem defined by the lines x1-x2=0 and x1+x2=1, represented by a four-node square-activation network.
evaluations.metric: Algebraic coefficient equality and an unquantified statement that softmax selects the intended class.
evaluations.result: A generic solver returns one set of weights for the two hand-specified quadratic class scores.
evaluations.baseline: No trained network, polynomial regression fit, held-out sample, or numerical accuracy baseline is reported.

evaluations.setting: Regression on the known quadratic r=2x1+2x1x2+x2 squared using the same four-node square-activation architecture.
evaluations.metric: Printed network output at two manually selected inputs.
evaluations.result: The code returns 5 at (1,1) and 9 at (2,1), matching the defining polynomial up to displayed precision.
evaluations.baseline: Direct evaluation of the same target polynomial; no noisy data, fitted baseline, or unseen-domain test.

evaluations.setting: A four-row, two-feature classification table with two examples per class and an eight-node fourth-power network.
evaluations.metric: Two output scores on the same four rows used to construct the class-distance polynomials.
evaluations.result: For each training row, the intended class score is approximately zero and the other is negative.
evaluations.baseline: No held-out data or ordinary classifier; this is interpolation of the construction set.

evaluations.setting: A symbolic proposal for fitting n regression observations with a univariate polynomial of one affine projection.
evaluations.metric: None beyond writing n nonlinear equations.
evaluations.result: No system is solved and no empirical result is reported.

limitations: Author-stated: the theory needs substantially more experiments, but the implementation work was not completed.
Author-stated: the one-dot categorical network is left entirely to future experimental work.
Reviewer inference: ReLU cannot equal one globally convergent power series across its kink, so the central exactness premise is false for the paper's main example activation.
Reviewer inference: compact polynomial approximation does not establish a unique, identifiable, or independently controllable infinite-dimensional representation.
Reviewer inference: no convergence radius, truncation error, preactivation-range bound, numerical conditioning, or degree-growth analysis is provided.
Reviewer inference: all numerical examples use finite monomial activations that the methodology initially excludes from its definition of modern activation functions.
Reviewer inference: the examples are target-designed interpolation identities and contain no evidence about learning from sampled data or generalization.
Reviewer inference: architecture conversion ignores coefficient-tensor rank, expressivity lower bounds, and the nonpolynomial piecewise structure of ReLU and max pooling.
Reviewer inference: the paper supplies no computational complexity result despite making a strong complexity-reduction claim.
Reviewer inference: the linked GitHub repository was unavailable at the checked URL on 2026-08-23.
failure_modes: Preactivations leave the interval on which the activation polynomial was fitted, causing rapidly growing approximation error.
A ReLU kink or max-pooling boundary is smoothed by the polynomial surrogate, changing the network's regions and decisions.
Degree grows explosively under composition, making explicit monomial expansion computationally and numerically infeasible.
The requested target coefficient tensor has rank larger than the selected hidden width, so coefficient matching has no solution.
The nonlinear system is underdetermined, singular, ill-conditioned, or traps a local root solver far from a useful solution.
Exact interpolation of constructed training points produces unstable extrapolation and no population accuracy.
A shallow replacement needs exponentially more units than the original deep network despite matching on a small sample.
Categorical values encoded as one scalar impose arbitrary ordinal polynomial geometry and fail under unseen categories.
reusable_insights: Activation expansions can expose which interaction orders a network emphasizes, but the basis, convergence domain, coefficient constraints, and truncation error must be explicit.
A network is linear in a lifted feature representation only after fixing that representation; this does not make its parameter optimization linear.
Coefficient tensors from powers of affine forms have low-rank structure, so tensor rank is the right feasibility test before promising architecture conversion.
Exact functional conversion, compact-domain approximation, and agreement on a finite dataset are three distinct compression objectives.
Piecewise-linear networks should be audited with polyhedral or spline tools rather than treated as globally analytic polynomials.
Constructive algebra examples need held-out error, range scaling, conditioning, solver success rates, and compute comparisons before supporting a learning claim.
A numerical root-finding reformulation is not a complexity reduction unless existence, runtime, accuracy, and scaling are established.
open_questions: Can activation expansions yield certified compact-domain error bounds that remain stable through many composed layers?
How does the symmetric tensor rank of a polynomial target determine the minimum width and depth of a polynomial-activation network?
Can a polynomial surrogate preserve every decision region of a trained ReLU network on a verified input domain?
When is coefficient matching better conditioned or faster than gradient training at realistic dimension and degree?
Can monomial or Hermite coefficients provide interpretable interaction summaries without explicitly materializing exponentially many features?
What architecture conversions are possible with provable approximation error and parameter growth under depth-width lower bounds?
How should category symmetries be represented so a polynomial model does not invent ordinal structure?
Does a learned polynomial surrogate retain calibration, robustness, and out-of-distribution behavior rather than only point predictions?

competitive_landscape.title: Toward Deeper Understanding of Neural Networks: The Power of Initialization and a Dual View on Expressivity
competitive_landscape.difference: Daniely, Frostig, and Singer develop a formal duality between network computation skeletons and compositional kernel Hilbert spaces, with activations expanded in an orthogonal basis and approximation theorems for random representations. This predates the Super Space intuition and supplies a function space, norm, assumptions, and finite-width approximation guarantees that the reviewed paper lacks.

competitive_landscape.title: Polynomial Networks and Factorization Machines: New Insights and Efficient Training Algorithms
competitive_landscape.difference: Blondel and colleagues formulate polynomial networks as low-rank symmetric tensor estimation and derive multi-convex training algorithms with real regression and recommendation experiments. Their tensor view makes explicit that monomial coefficients are constrained by rank and width, directly exposing the missing feasibility condition in arbitrary Super Plane matching.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Expressive Power of Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Raghu and colleagues quantify trajectory length and activation-pattern complexity as functions of depth and show depth can create much greater complexity than width. The reviewed paper collapses depth into an unspecified polynomial expansion and therefore misses the parameter blow-up that can prevent compression into a chosen shallow architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Polynomial Regression As an Alternative to Neural Nets
competitive_landscape.difference: Cheng and colleagues already argue that neural networks are approximately polynomial regression models and empirically compare an implemented polynomial method against networks. The reviewed paper adds Super Space terminology and coefficient-solving toys, but does not establish a stronger exact equivalence or reproduce the predecessor's real comparative evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: ReLU Deep Neural Networks and Linear Finite Elements
competitive_landscape.difference: He and colleagues treat ReLU networks as continuous piecewise-linear functions, give exact finite-element constructions, and prove layer requirements for representing general piecewise-linear functions. That exact polyhedral account is compatible with ReLU's kink; the reviewed paper's globally polynomial Super Plane is not.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards a mathematical framework to inform Neural Network modelling via Polynomial Regression
competitive_landscape.relationship: cited direct predecessor with error conditions
competitive_landscape.difference: Morala and colleagues derive explicit polynomial coefficients from one-hidden-layer regression networks using Taylor expansion and empirically test when predictions agree, explicitly conditioning validity on preactivation distributions and activations. The reviewed paper generalizes rhetorically to arbitrary deep networks but omits comparable range constraints and approximation-error measurements.

competitive_landscape.title: Width is Less Important than Depth in ReLU Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Vardi, Yehudai, and Shamir prove approximation of arbitrary target networks by narrow deep ReLU networks with explicit width, depth, parameter, and error costs, while noting depth-separation barriers to reversing the trade. This is the kind of qualified conversion theorem needed for compression; it contradicts an unrestricted conversion into any desired one- or two-layer architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Fast Neural Kernel Embeddings for General Activations
competitive_landscape.difference: Han and colleagues approximate multilayer NNGP and neural tangent kernels for general activations with truncated Hermite expansions, deriving sketch dimensions and runtime and reporting large measured speedups. It turns activation series into controlled finite embeddings; the reviewed paper provides neither an orthogonality measure nor truncation and propagation guarantees.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Geometry and Optimization of Polynomial Convolutional Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Shahverdi, Marchetti, and Kohn study convolutional networks with monomial activations through the dimension, degree, singularities, and optimization geometry of the resulting neuromanifold. Their image-variety analysis precisely distinguishes representable coefficient tensors from the full polynomial space, a distinction erased by Super Plane terminology.

competitive_landscape.title: A Depth Hierarchy for Computing the Maximum in ReLU Networks via Extremal Graph Theory
competitive_landscape.relationship: current lower bound relevant to max pooling
competitive_landscape.difference: Safran proves depth-dependent width lower bounds for exact maximum computation, showing that even this simple nonsmooth operation has architecture-sensitive complexity. The reviewed paper merely labels max pooling another polynomial approximation and therefore cannot justify exact or efficient architecture-independent compression.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Nonlinear activations exactly magnify an ordinary input space into a previously unreported infinite monomial Super Space, every activated neuron is a Super Plane in it, and this equivalence enables arbitrary model compression and training by nonlinear coefficient equations.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper supplies a Fourier-then-Taylor approximation sketch, formal monomial notation, three hand-constructed coefficient-solving examples, and one unsolved symbolic example.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Little defensible novelty remains after primary comparison. Infinite activation-induced feature spaces, kernel duality, polynomial surrogates, polynomial networks, tensor-rank constraints, and exact ReLU piecewise-linear representations all predate this paper. Its new terminology packages a reasonable compact-domain approximation intuition as an invalid exact global claim, while the compression and complexity conclusions are neither proved nor tested. A viable contribution would need bounded-domain error propagation, coefficient-rank feasibility, architecture-size guarantees, solver complexity, and evaluations on actual trained deep networks.

reviewer_notes: Read all 13 pages, including every displayed equation, all three diagrams, the four experiment sections, printed Octave snippets, conclusion, and references. The visual audit confirmed that Figures 1 through 3 are conceptual/network schematics rather than empirical plots and that the only table has four construction rows. The paper-linked GitHub repository returned 404 on 2026-08-23, so no external implementation remained to inspect. The contradiction audit distinguishes valid compact polynomial approximation from unsupported exact equality, arbitrary architecture conversion, and complexity reduction. Primary arXiv, NeurIPS, ICML, COLT, AISTATS, and PMLR records were researched through 2026-08-23.
